question: What do the Israelites ask the LORD after the death of Joshua, and what answer do they receive?
What does Adoni-bezek recognize about what happened to him, and what idea of justice appears in his words?
Several tribes make the Canaanites מַס (mas, “forced laborers”) instead of driving them out: what does this solution reveal about the people's priorities?
Judah did not drive out the people of the plains because “they had iron chariots”: what obstacles usually make you stop halfway through a task?
What does the angel of the LORD say at Bochim, and how do the people react?
What does it mean that “another generation arose who knew neither the LORD nor the work” He had done for Israel?
What did the judges raised up by the LORD do, according to vv. 16-19, and in what way does the verb שָׁפַט (shafat, “judge, govern”) go beyond the work of a court?
The people improve while the judge lives and become corrupt after he dies: on whom or what does your faithfulness to God depend?
Who is Othniel, and what happens when the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him?
How do you read Ehud's cunning and violence, and why does the text make a point of saying he was left-handed?
Othniel, Ehud and Shamgar “save” Israel, with the verb יָשַׁע (yasha‘, “save, deliver”): who, according to the chapter, is the author of this salvation?
The cycle of forgetting, serving other gods, suffering and crying out appears here for the first time: what do you usually forget when things are going well?
Who is Deborah, and what did she do under the palm tree between Ramah and Bethel?
Why does Barak demand that Deborah go with him, and what does she answer about the honor of the victory?
The nine hundred iron רֶכֶב (rekhev, “chariots”) were Sisera's strength: what happens to them in the battle, and what does this suggest?
“Has not the LORD gone before you?”: in what decision do you need to hear someone encourage you to rise up?
Which tribes does the song praise for going to battle, and which does it rebuke for staying behind?
What is the effect of the song ending with Sisera's mother at the window, waiting for a son who will not return?
The song praises the people who “offered themselves willingly,” with the verb נָדַב (nadav, “volunteer, offer oneself”): what place does this willingness have in the victory celebrated?
Deborah says she arose “a mother in Israel”: who has been a presence like that for you, rising up when everything seemed stalled?
Where is Gideon and what is he doing when the angel appears, and how does he respond to the greeting?
Why is Gideon's first task to tear down his father's altar of Baal, and what does the name Jerubbaal mean?
How do you understand the request for a sign with the גָּזַּה (gazzah, “fleece”), if God had already promised to be with Gideon?
Gideon sees himself as the least in the poorest family: what does the answer “I will be with you” say to you when you feel too small for a task?
How is Gideon's army reduced, and how many men are left in the end?
What reason does God give for reducing the army, and what does He want to avoid?
Trumpets, torches and the broken כַּד (kad, “jar”): what kind of weapons do the three hundred use, and what does this say about the victory?
God offers Gideon a way to overcome fear by going down to the enemy camp: what has God already used to strengthen you before a difficult decision?
How do the men of Succoth and Penuel respond to Gideon's request for bread, and what does he promise to do?
Why does Gideon refuse to be king, and how does this refusal compare with what he does right afterward with the gold?
In a book that asks who should rule Israel, what does the phrase “the LORD will rule over you” mean, said with the verb מָשַׁל (mashal, “rule, govern”)?
Right after Gideon's death, the people forget the LORD and the house of Jerubbaal: how do you keep the memory of those who helped you?
How does Abimelech come to power in Shechem, and with what resources?
What does Jotham's fable say about who accepts to reign and who refuses, and who would the thornbush be?
Why do the useful עֵץ (‘ets, “trees”), like the olive, the fig and the vine, refuse the crown, and what does this image suggest about power?
The text says God brought the evil back on Abimelech and on the men of Shechem: how do you react when it seems that injustice is winning?
Who were Tola and Jair, and what does the text record about each one?
Why does the LORD first say He will not deliver them anymore, and what changes in v. 16?
The people עָזַב (‘azav, “forsook”) the LORD, and the LORD speaks of no longer delivering: what does this verb reveal about the broken relationship?
“We have sinned; do to us whatever seems good to You”: what would a repentance that does not try to bargain with God look like for you?
Who is Jephthah, and why was he driven out by his brothers?
What arguments does Jephthah present to the king of the Ammonites before going to war?
How do you read Jephthah's vow, and what does it reveal about the way he understood God?
What does the story show about the danger of a vow made with the verb נָדַר (nadar, “vow”) without weighing the consequences, and how should it be read alongside Deuteronomy 12:31?
Jephthah's daughter is remembered every year by the young women of Israel: what innocent people, struck by the decisions of others, should you not forget?
What do the men of Ephraim accuse Jephthah of, and how does he respond?
What does the “Shibboleth” episode show about the division between the tribes of Israel?
The מַעֲבָר (ma‘avar, “ford”) of the Jordan, a place for crossing, becomes a place of death: what contrast does the text create with this word?
A difference in pronunciation decided who lived: what small differences do you usually use to separate “us” and “them”?
What does the angel announce to Manoah's wife, and what instructions does he give her?
How does Manoah's wife reason in the face of her husband's fear, and what does this show about her?
The angel says his name is פִּלְאִי (pil'i, “beyond understanding, wonderful”): why does he not reveal the name, and what link does this word have with Isaiah 9:6?
Manoah asks the messenger to come back and “teach us” what to do with the boy: what help do you ask of God to care for the people entrusted to you?
What does Samson ask of his parents, and how do they react?
How does the text relate Samson's choice to the LORD's plan against the Philistines, and how should this statement be read?
How does the חִידָה (chidah, “riddle”) arise from something only Samson saw, and what does the way it is revealed say about the characters?
Samson's wife is pressured with threats and pressures her husband with tears: how do you deal with pressure coming from several sides?
What does Samson do with the foxes, and why?
Why do the men of Judah hand Samson over to the Philistines, and what does this reveal about the people's situation?
The verb קָרָא (qara', “call, cry out”) appears when Samson names the place and when he cries out to the LORD in thirst: what link does the text suggest between the two moments?
After a great victory, Samson finds himself on the verge of dying of thirst: how do you deal with the exhaustion that comes after a great effort?
Who is Delilah, and what do the rulers of the Philistines propose to her?
What does v. 20 reveal about Samson at the moment he wakes up thinking he would escape as at other times?
The word פַּעַם (pa‘am, “time”) marks Delilah's attempts and Samson's last prayer (v. 28): what rhythm does this word give the story?
Blind and humiliated, Samson prays “remember me”: what does this prayer say to you about seeking God even after great failures?
What happens to the eleven hundred shekels of silver, and what does Micah's mother do with part of them?
How does v. 6 sum up the atmosphere of these final chapters, and what relation does it have with what Micah does?
The silver is “consecrated to the LORD” and becomes a פֶּסֶל (pesel, “carved image”): what does this mixture reveal about Micah's religion?
“Now I know that the LORD will be good to me, because a Levite has become my priest”: in what ways might you try to secure God's blessing by your own means?
Why does the tribe of Dan send spies, and what do they find at Laish?
What leads the Levite to abandon Micah and go with the Danites, and what does this show about his calling?
What role do the תְּרָפִים (terafim, “household idols”) and the ephod have in the story, and what happens to them?
Micah laments: “You took the gods I made”: in what have you placed your security that could be taken away at any moment?
How are the Levite and his concubine received in Gibeah, and who finally takes them in?
What parallels does the account of Gibeah have with that of Sodom (Gen 19), and what does this say about Israel at that time?
The verb לוּן (lun, “spend the night”) is repeated from beginning to end of the chapter: how does the search for a safe place to spend the night end in tragedy?
The woman has no voice in the account and no one protects her: how do you read this silence, and what responsibility does it awaken in you toward victims of violence today?
How do the tribes react to the Levite's account, and where do they gather?
Why is Israel defeated twice even after inquiring of God, and what changes at the third inquiry?
The word רַע (ra‘, “evil”) names the crime of Gibeah and also what falls on Benjamin (vv. 34 and 41): how does evil multiply throughout the chapter?
The Benjamites refuse to hand over the guilty: in what situation could loyalty to your group keep you from facing a serious wrong?
What oath had the men of Israel taken, and why do they now weep before God?
How do you evaluate the solutions found to provide wives for the Benjamites, and what do they reveal about the state of the people?
What does the chapter show about the decisions made in the name of the whole עֵדָה (‘edah, “congregation”)?
The book ends with “everyone did what was right in his own eyes”: where do you notice this way of living today, including in yourself?
